part2.sample:
I'm going to talk about a man called Mr Halloran, who lived two doors down from us when I was about thirteen. He was a retired engineer, and his garage was always full of bits of bicycles – old frames hanging from the ceiling, boxes of gears, that kind of thing.

The skill he taught me was how to repair and look after a bike. It actually started by accident. I got a puncture right outside his house, and instead of just fixing it for me, he handed me the tools and talked me through it. After that, I'd pop round most Saturday mornings, and over a couple of years he showed me how to adjust brakes, replace a chain and straighten a wheel.

What I really appreciated was the way he taught. He never took over, even when I was obviously making a mess of things. He'd just ask questions like, 'So what do you think that spring is for?' until I worked it out for myself. To be honest, it drove me mad at the time, but it meant I genuinely understood what I was doing rather than just copying him.

As for how it's been useful – well, I cycle to university every day, so it saves me quite a bit of money, because I hardly ever need to take my bike to a shop. More importantly, though, it gave me the confidence to have a go at fixing other things, like a dripping tap, instead of immediately calling someone. So I'd say he taught me far more than just how to fix bikes.

part2.sample:
I'd like to talk about a spot by the river just outside my home town. Locals call it Willow Bend, because the river curves sharply there and the banks are lined with these enormous old willow trees.

It's only about fifteen minutes from my flat by bike. You follow a cycle path along the edge of some fields, and then, quite suddenly, the noise of the traffic disappears and all you can hear is the water and the birds.

What I do there really depends on the season. In summer, I usually go with a couple of friends in the early evening, once it's a bit cooler. We take some food, sit on the grass and sometimes paddle in the shallow part, although the water's freezing even in July. In winter, I tend to go on my own, usually on a Sunday morning, just to walk along the bank and clear my head. I often take a book, but to be honest I rarely read much of it – I end up just watching the water.

As for why I enjoy it so much, I think it's mainly the contrast with the rest of my week. I spend most of my time in front of a screen, either studying or working, and being by the water seems to slow everything down. It's hard to put into words, but I always come back feeling calmer and better able to concentrate. It's also full of memories for me, because my dad used to take me fishing there when I was small, so in a way it feels like part of my childhood.

part2.sample:
I'd like to talk about a pair of leather walking boots that I had repaired last winter, instead of throwing them away.

I bought them about six years ago, just before a hiking trip, and they were quite expensive – probably the most I'd ever spent on shoes. I've worn them on almost every walk since then, so they've been through a lot: mud, snow, rocky paths, you name it. Last year, though, the sole on the left boot started coming away at the front, and water was getting in, which isn't ideal when you're halfway up a hill in the rain.

My first instinct was just to buy a new pair, but a friend told me about a tiny shoe-repair shop near the station, run by an elderly man who's apparently been doing the job for about forty years. I took them in, and he replaced both soles, restitched a couple of seams and even polished the leather. It took about a week and cost roughly a third of the price of new boots.

So why did I repair them? Well, money was the obvious reason, but there was more to it than that. Boots like that take ages to break in, and these fitted my feet perfectly, so I didn't want to start all over again. I also feel slightly guilty about how much we throw away these days, and it seemed wasteful to get rid of something that was basically still in good condition. And honestly, I'm quite attached to them – they've been with me on some of my best trips, so keeping them felt a bit like holding on to an old friend.

part2.sample:
The ceremony I'm going to talk about is my graduation from university, which was about two years ago now, in early July.

It took place in the university's main hall, which is a beautiful old building with a high painted ceiling and wood-panelled walls. There must have been around four hundred graduates there that day, all in black gowns and mortarboards, which never seem to stay on properly.

My parents came, of course, along with my grandmother, who'd travelled for nearly five hours to be there, which meant a lot to me. A couple of my closest friends were graduating at the same time, so we sat together and kept making each other laugh during the speeches, which probably wasn't very respectful!

The ceremony itself was quite formal. The head of the university gave a speech, and then each of us had to walk across the stage when our name was read out, shake hands and collect our certificate. I remember being terrified that I'd trip on the steps in front of everyone.

As for why it was so important to me – well, I was the first person in my family to go to university, so it didn't feel like my achievement alone. It felt as if it belonged to my parents as well, because they'd made a lot of sacrifices to support me. Seeing my dad, who isn't usually an emotional person, wiping his eyes is something I'll never forget. It also marked the end of a really happy chapter of my life and the start of working life, so I'd say it was a strange mixture of pride and sadness.

part2.sample:
I'm going to describe a journey I made about three years ago, when I was going to the coast to visit an old school friend who'd just moved there.

The plan couldn't have been simpler. I was going by train, on a direct line, so it should have taken just under three hours. I'd booked an early train so that we'd have the whole afternoon to explore the town.

Things started going wrong about an hour into the journey. The train stopped in the middle of nowhere, and after about twenty minutes the driver announced that a tree had come down across the line in a storm the night before. We sat there for nearly two hours, and eventually we were taken back to the previous station and put on a replacement bus. Then, of course, the bus got stuck in heavy traffic, because everyone else was trying to get round the same problem. In the end, I arrived at about eight in the evening – almost nine hours after I'd set off.

How did I feel? Well, at first I was fairly relaxed, because I had a book and some snacks. But by the time we were on the bus, I was getting really frustrated, especially as my phone battery was almost dead and I couldn't keep my friend updated. That said, looking back, it wasn't all bad. I got chatting to an elderly couple sitting next to me, who were hilarious, and they even shared their sandwiches with me. So it's turned into one of those stories I actually enjoy telling, even though I certainly didn't enjoy living through it!

part2.sample:
I'd like to talk about a podcast I've been listening to for about two years now. It's called Next Door, Far Away, and it's presented by two former teachers who travel to different countries and talk to ordinary people about their daily lives – farmers, bus drivers, students, that sort of thing.

Each episode is around forty minutes long and focuses on one place. So one week they might be in a fishing village, and the next they'll be following a nurse on a night shift in a big city. What makes it different from a typical travel programme is that they hardly ever mention tourist attractions. It's much more about how people live, what worries them and what they hope for.

I actually came across it by chance. I was on a long coach journey and I'd run out of things to listen to, so I just picked something from the recommended list – and ended up listening to four episodes in a row!

These days I usually listen while I'm cooking or on my way to work, so it fits neatly into my routine and never feels like a waste of time.

The main reason I keep following it is that it's so human. You hear people's real voices, and you realise that people in completely different situations have a lot in common. It's also done wonders for my listening skills, because the presenters have quite different accents, and they explain things clearly without oversimplifying them. I've recommended it to quite a few friends, and most of them are hooked now as well.
